entries.title: Heavy rain, flash flooding possible in Chicago area overnight
entries.summary: <p>Heavy rain and thunderstorms could bring flash flooding to the Chicago area overnight Sunday, with forecasters most concerned about the period from about 10 or 11 p.m. through early Monday.</p><p>A flood watch issued Sunday afternoon remains in effect until 7 a.m. Monday, according to the National Weather Service.</p><p>Showers and thunderstorms were developing across northwest Illinois and moving into the area Sunday evening, said Mike Bardou, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service.</p><p>The storms could bring multiple rounds of heavy rainfall to some areas, Bardou said. It remained unclear Sunday evening which areas would receive the most rain.</p><p>The heaviest rainfall in the Chicago area could begin between about 10 p.m. and midnight and continue for several hours overnight, Bardou said.</p><p>“Flash flooding is one of our biggest concerns here because the rain could fall very quickly, in the order of 1 to 2 inches per hour under some of these storms, or even perhaps briefly heavier than that,” Bardou said.</p><p>Some parts of the Chicago area, including many suburbs, had already received 1 to 3 inches of rain earlier Sunday, leaving some areas saturated and potentially with standing water, Bardou said.</p><p>The weather could also affect the Monday morning commute. Bardou said the bulk of the rainfall would probably occur before daybreak, but ponding or flooding could persist into the morning, depending on how much rain falls and where.</p><p>Bardou pointed to viaducts in the city, typical high-water areas and some expressways as places where flooding or ponding could potentially linger. Damaging winds are also a concern. </p><p>The weather service issued a severe thunderstorm watch at 8:44 p.m. Sunday for Cook, DuPage and several other Illinois counties. The watch remains in effect until 4 a.m. Monday.</p><p>Bardou said damaging straight-line winds and large hail were also concerns.</p><p>“The biggest thing is it’s a good evening and overnight to stay weather aware and have a way to get woken up by warnings if you’re going to be asleep,” Bardou said.</p><p>He also urged people who live near creeks that rise quickly or in areas prone to basement flooding to monitor conditions and have a way to receive warning notifications.</p><p>As of 9:40 p.m. Sunday, ComEd reported 288 active outages affecting more than 7,900 customers.</p>

entries.title: Man fatally shot in head in Englewood
entries.summary: <p>A man was fatally struck in the head by gunfire in Englewood Sunday afternoon and taken to the University of Chicago Medical Center, Chicago police said.</p><p>The victim was pronounced at the hospital, police said.</p><p>The victim had in the 1300 block of West 73rd Place in the Englewood neighborhood at about 4:19 p.m. when he was struck in the head by gunfire, police said.</p><p>The victim’s age remained unknown Sunday evening.</p><p>Police said there were no updates available, and the shooting remained under investigation by area detectives.</p>

entries.title: Hagen Smith earns first major-league victory in first appearance for White Sox
entries.summary: <p>Left-hander Hagen Smith earned his first major-league victory in his first major-league appearance in the oddest of ways.</p><p>The Guardians and White Sox played the first inning of their series finale Sunday at Rate Field before the heavens unexpectedly opened. Major League Baseball and the Sox saw forecasts that called for clear skies, despite heavy rain to the north. After another rough first inning for right-hander Davis Martin, his day was done.</p><p>With four lefties and four switch hitters in the Guardians’ lineup, Sox manager Will Venable chose Smith to take the ball after the rain delay, which lasted 2 hours and 23 minutes.</p><p>“I didn’t know I was going in till about an hour into the delay,” Smith said. “I was like, ‘Sounds good to me.’ ”</p><p>And it looked good to the Sox. Smith struck out the side in the second inning before walking the bases loaded in the third and escaping. When the Sox scored four runs in their third, on the strength of Colson Montgomery’s three-run homer, Smith was in line for the win.</p><p>He got it when the Sox held on for a 5-3 victory, taking the series and extending their lead in the American League Central to a season-high 3 ½ games, only now it’s over the Tigers, who are a half-game ahead of the Twins and Guardians. The Sox visit the Tigers next weekend.</p><p>The victory also gave the Sox 61 wins, one more than they had all of last season.</p><p>“It’s great. It signals progress for us,” manager Will Venable said. “Obviously, we have a long way to go here, but certainly happy about where we’re at now, knowing that we’ve gone through some stuff and continue to push through and just get better and better.”</p><p>The Sox called up Smith, along with right-hander Tanner McDougal, on Saturday. Smith, the Sox’ No. 2 prospect and 51st-ranked prospect overall, according to MLB.com, struck out 87 hitters in 58 ⅓ innings at Triple-A Charlotte this season, allowing only a .189 batting average. But he also walked 40. On Sunday, he struck out three and walked four.</p><p>“He’s got such good stuff,” Venable said. “If he’s in the zone, he’s going to be really hard to deal with. We saw that, and you understand with that stuff, it’s hard to control the movement, that there are going to be some walks in there. But as he continues to grow, you expect him to be able to tighten it up.”</p><p>“The first inning obviously was good, and then the second inning fell off a little bit,” Smith said. “You just want to go out there and compete, and the results are what they are. And it turned out to be good.”</p><p>The Sox drafted Smith fifth overall out of Arkansas in 2024. He rose through the organization each season before getting the call.</p><p>“You always dream of this growing up, especially when you get drafted,” he said. “You just look forward to the debut. It was a really special moment.”</p><p>“You have these plans to get these young guys a nice soft landing spot,” Venable said, “and the second inning after a rain delay is not something he’s done before. And then as his outing unfolded, he was challenged in his second inning with the bases loaded. It was a really good test for him and obviously came through.”</p><p>McDougal almost had his special moment, too. With righty Trevor Richards, the Sox’ seventh pitcher of the game, struggling in the ninth, Venable had McDougal warming up. Richards walked No. 9 hitter Angel Genao to start the inning, then walked Chase DeLauter one out later, bringing up Jose Ramirez as the tying run.</p><p>Ramirez hit a sacrifice fly, and Rhys Hoskins flew out to end it, giving Richards his first save of the season and third of his career — and Smith his first victory.</p><p>“I didn’t know that until I got back in the clubhouse,” Smith said.</p><div class="PageListL" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" data-show-loadmore="true" ><a class="AnchorLink" id="list-4a0005" entries.title: Bally’s to stop work on some amenities at permanent Chicago casino development amid video gambling dispute
entries.summary: <p>Bally’s is “resetting the pace of construction” on parts of its permanent Chicago casino development in River West, the company said Sunday.</p><p>The announcement comes amid an ongoing dispute over the potential expansion of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/06/29/ballys-casino-river-west-lori-lightfoot-lawsuit-challenge-video-gambling-terminals" target="_blank" ><u>video gambling terminals</u></a> in the city.</p><p>Bally’s notified the Chicago Community Builders Collective on Saturday that work would stop on some of the surrounding amenities, including the hotel, event center and some restaurants.</p><p>Subcontractors were informed Sunday morning, a spokesperson said, and the work stoppage would most likely take effect Monday.</p><p>The opening of the permanent casino remains set for early 2027, the company said.</p><p>Bally’s said the city had also been alerted to the announcement.</p><p>The company said in a statement that the potential for an “uncontrolled proliferation” of video gambling terminals breaches the city’s commitment not to expand gaming under its host community agreement with Bally’s and “creates uncertainty” that could hurt the casino’s prospects.</p><p>The $16.6 billion 2026 city budget lifted Chicago’s ban on video gambling terminals. Bally’s has opposed their legalization in the city, arguing it violates the host agreement.</p><p>The $1.7 billion casino project has encountered financial and logistical challenges since Bally’s was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2022/5/25/23141244/ballys-casino-approved-chicago-city-council-river-west-medinah-temple-lightfoot-police-fire-pensions" target="_blank" ><u>selected</u></a> to build Chicago’s casino in 2022, including an <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/casinos-gambling/2024/03/12/ballys-chicago-casino-buyout-soo-kim" target="_blank" ><u>$800 million</u></a> “funding gap,” <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2024/1/22/24047289/ballys-casino-hotel-tower-plans-changes-city-hall-chicago-river" target="_blank" ><u>changes to its hotel plans</u></a> and delays that pushed the permanent casino’s expected opening into 2027.</p><p>Bally’s said Sunday the company intends to fully honor its commitments under the host agreement.</p><p>The company acknowledged the construction changes would affect many of the 1,500 union workers affiliated with the project but did not specify exactly how many would be impacted.</p><p>“We do not take this lightly because of the potential impact on many of the 1,500 union tradespeople who have been working hard to build Bally’s Chicago,” Bally’s said.</p><p>The company did not provide a timeline for when work on the affected portions of the development could resume.</p><p>Bally’s said it would continue assessing its options, which the company said it hopes will include “more productive discussions with the Mayor’s Office and City Council.”</p><p>Mayor Brandon Johnson has previously <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/06/29/ballys-casino-river-west-lori-lightfoot-lawsuit-challenge-video-gambling-terminals" target="_blank" ><u>expressed concerns</u></a> that entries.title: 2 teens wounded in Washington Park shooting
entries.summary: <p>Two 17-year-old boys were wounded in a shooting in Washington Park Sunday afternoon, Chicago police said.</p><p>The boys were in an alley along the 5900 block of South Michigan Avenue at about 1:30 p.m. when the shooting took place, police said. </p><p>The first victim was shot in the hand and the second victim suffered a gunshot wound to the leg, according to police.</p><p>The first boy was taken to Comer Children’s Hospital while the second was taken to the University of Chicago Medical Center, police said.</p><p>Both boys were reported in good condition.</p><p>Area detectives are investigating.</p>

entries.title: Decades-old mistreatment of Japanese Americans reverberates with country's current policies
entries.summary: <p>The fear over Japan's attack on Pearl Harbor led to the signing of <a class="Link" href="https://www.archives.gov/milestone-documents/executive-order-9066" target="_blank" >Executive Order 9066</a> on Feb. 19, 1942, permitting the forced removal of all people of Japanese descent from their West Coast homes and into assembly centers and concentration camps. The 10 concentration camps that were constructed imprisoned 126,000 Japanese — two-thirds who were U.S. citizens.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://savingplaces.org/places/tule-lake" target="_blank" >Tule Lake</a> Segregation Center was the largest camp. It held 18,700 adults and children in a squalid overcrowded space designed to accommodate 15,000 prisoners. Just last month, the nonprofit <a class="Link" href="https://www.tulelake.org/" target="_blank" >Tule Lake Committee</a> organized its biannual four-day pilgrimage to Tule Lake, California, for descendants and survivors of this ugly chapter in American history.</p><p>Toward the end of the war, Tule Lake is where the U.S. Department of Justice set in motion an unprecedented plan that enabled the deportation of "disloyal" Japanese Americans. Public Law 78-805 was drafted on July 1, 1944, permitting U.S. citizens to renounce their citizenship. Many Japanese Americans were misled, believing if they renounced their citizenship, their families could remain together in protective custody at Tule Lake. Horribly, misinformation drove 5,461 Japanese Americans to give up their seemingly worthless birthright citizenship at Tule Lake.</p><p>Without the protection of U.S. citizenship, several thousand young men were separated from their families and interned as "enemy aliens" and deported to DOJ internment camps. The decision to give up birthright citizenship was an act done under duress, and nearly all who renounced sought restoration of their citizenship, which the Justice Department refused.</p><p>Fortunately, civil rights lawyer <a class="Link" href="http://remembrance-project.janm.org/tributes/wayne-collins.html" target="_blank" >Wayne M. Collins</a>, through his advocacy, stopped the involuntary deportations and restored citizenship to nearly all those Japanese Americans who were stripped of their birthright. But in spite of the reversal of the deportations, those who renounced their citizenship encountered decades of shame and rejection within the Japanese community.</p><p>Forty-six years after the wartime incarceration, our government <a class="Link" href="https://www.archives.gov/press/press-releases/2013/nr13-118.html" target="_blank" >recognized the error of its actions </a>with a presidential apology, redress and reparation payments to survivors.</p><p>Today's mass deportations, inhumane imprisonment conditions and attacks on birthright citizenship echo the unjust treatment experienced by Japanese Americans during World War II. When will we stop making the same grievous mistakes?</p><p><i>Michael Harada, Wilmette</i><br><i>Barbara Takei, Sacramento, California</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-f20000" name="module-f20000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Give us your take</h3><br>Send letters to the editor to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. To be considered for publication, letters must include your full name, your neighborhood or hometown and a phone number for verification purposes. Letters should be a maximum of approximately 375 words.</div> </div><p></p><h3>Aiming high for state’s Department of Natural Resources</h3><p>Gov. JB Pritzker has built one of the <a class="Link" href="https://rmi.org/resources/state-climate-action-updated-scorecards-tracking-progress-to-2030/" target="_blank" >strongest climate action records in the country</a> and now has the chance to make it even stronger. Healthy, resilient nature is a key part of the equation, one that can drive more economic investment. A transformational appointment for the next director of the <a class="Link" href="https://dnr.illinois.gov/" target="_blank" >Illinois Department of Natural Resources</a> can extend his leadership through visionary investment in nature.</p><p>The department's mission is to steward the state’s natural resources for the health of ecosystems and the well-being of residents. That extends beyond state parks to ensuring that all of Illinois’ lands and waters are healthy and beautiful.</p><p>People choose where to live based on quality of life. Access to parks, trails, clean water and vibrant natural areas is exactly what makes a place feel compelling. It's why families put down roots and why young professionals choose one city over another. Businesses know this, too. When they're deciding where to locate and how to attract talent, they look for places their employees want to live.</p><p>As a former chair of the Forest Preserves of Cook County’s Conservation and Policy Council, I saw firsthand how good leadership can nurture the land and local communities. Deer Grove East Forest Preserve is one such success story. An <a class="Link" href="https://openlands.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/05/rpt_dge_econ_valuation_final_10102016.pdf" target="_blank" >economic analysis of the restoration work</a> found that every dollar spent on restoration delivered an immediate $2 return from jobs and economic activity. In the long term, it delivered a whopping $6 return from flood control, water quality benefits and recreational activity. At the scale of the state, the health and economic benefits of this type of conservation are indisputable.</p><p>Cook County voters understand this and responded in 2022 by passing, with an <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagotribune.com/2023/10/17/cook-county-forest-preserves-189-million-budget-marks-new-era-with-referendum-cash/" target="_blank" >overwhelming majority, a ballot measure</a> that increases investment in nature by $45 million a year. The five collar counties followed suit in 2024, generating over $1 billion over the next 20 years for nature.</p><p>There’s real headroom here. Illinois has lost more than 99% of the state’s original prairie and over 85% of its historic wetlands, and ranks 49th in the nation in protected natural areas per capita — a clear marker of fragmented habitats. As climate change reshapes ecosystems across the country, Illinois has the chance to step up and lead.</p><p>We love the Prairie State. The governor loves it, too. A transformational appointment for the Illinois Department of Natural Resources is his opportunity to write the next chapter of that legacy.</p><p><i>Wendy J. Paulson, executive chairwoman, Bobolink Foundation</i></p><h3>Trump doesn’t deserve to be called a leader</h3><h3></h3><p>I take issue with David McGrath's recent op-ed headlined <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/other-views/2026/07/31/president-donald-trump-cold-blooded-leader-death-iran-ice-shootings-covid-measles-david-mcgrath" target="_blank" >“Trump is our cold-blooded leader.”</a> I do not take issue with the atrocities and unlawfulness McGrath noted about the Trump administration. However, I disagree with his describing Trump as a "leader."</p><p>According to Merriam-Webster, leadership means "the office or position of a leader," "a capacity to lead" and "the act or instance of leading." I fail to see any "leadership" qualities — as well as integrity, honesty, accountability, responsibility, empathy, compassion — in Trump as he's pushed the country to the economic brink with his tariffs, endangered us in an unwinnable war in the Middle East and dismissed higher education and science as the bases of government.</p><p>Words have meaning, as McGrath surely knows. I think we need to be careful in calling Trump a "leader." I describe him as the "occupier" of the White House, but I'll leave it up to Professor McGrath to find a more appropriate moniker or epithet.</p><p><i>Linda Hendelman, West Ridge</i></p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Cruise with friends could wind up far from paradise
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My husband and I have friends who are kind, intelligent and warm. However, as we have spent more time with them, "Phyllis'" compulsive talking has become a real problem for us. She hijacks whichever one of us is sitting next to her and starts a monologue that goes on and on.</p><p>Phyllis doesn't even look at the person she's talking to and doesn't hear when you try to interject anything. She has said she's hard of hearing and does wear a hearing aid, but I believe the problem is more than a hearing deficit.</p><p>The dilemma is they have booked a cruise with us. We didn't ask them to, but when I mentioned we were going, they thought it would be fun. The thought of having dinner together every night and being subjected to this is going to put a distinct damper on what is a rare vacation for my husband and me. Is there any way to not offend them and have more give-and-take in the conversation? — <i>DREADING IT IN OREGON</i></p><p><b>DEAR DREADING IT:</b> You or your husband need to make clear to this couple well before the ship sets sail that you signed up for this cruise because you want to spend time alone together, meet new people and make new friends, which is why you will not be able to dine with them every night or participate in every activity with them. Period.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My wife of 48 years recently died, and my stepson put some artificial flowers on her grave. I was surprised to see this when I visited on the eight-month anniversary of her death. Both my wife and I always considered artificial flowers tacky and not appropriate for cemeteries, even though lots of people decorate gravesites with them.</p><p>I haven't said anything to him about my feelings about plastic flowers, but I would like to prevent more of them from being placed when these fade away. How can I ask him to not put any more plastic flowers on the grave, or should I just ignore it? I'm less likely to visit her grave when these flowers are there. — <i>MOURNING IN ALABAMA</i></p><p><b>DEAR MOURNING:</b> Your stepson may not realize how his mother felt about plastic flowers, so mention it to him the next time you talk. If he doesn't visit his mother's grave often, he may not realize that they have been removed, which I suggest you do if seeing them would discourage your visits.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I've been married for 40 years, but it's a platonic relationship with no communication on his part. I must run the household, make sure bills get paid and be responsible for everything — whatever life throws at us. My health is waning, and I'm concerned for my future. I have tried talking, counseling, etc., to no avail. What do I do? — <i>FED UP IN UTAH</i></p><p><b>DEAR FED UP:</b> Because, after 40 years, you are finally fed up enough that you might actually do something about it, I'm suggesting some sessions with a different counselor than the one you have been seeing. You stated that you are the one who takes care of the house, pays the bills, etc. Has your husband been earning the money? If so, then you might also benefit from interviewing several attorneys about what your options might be if you no longer wish to carry the whole load alone.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren, also known as Jeanne Phillips, and was founded by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 69440, Los Angeles, CA 90069.</i></p>

entries.title: CPS budget challenges Springfield to pay up
entries.summary: <p>Unless you’ve been living under a rock, you know the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-school-board/2026/07/30/chicago-school-board-approves-budget-that-reverses-layoffs-but-counts-on-shaky-state-funds" >$9.96 billion budget Chicago Public Schools passed</a> for the coming fiscal year is generating some controversy. OK, so whenever CPS does anything it engenders controversy. But in this case, some legitimate issues are on the table.</p><p>That’s because in a split vote, the CPS Board passed a budget that includes <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/08/04/mayor-brandon-johnson-cps-budget-schools-funding-tif-surplus-springfield-state-funding" >$150 million in state funding</a> the Illinois<b> </b>General Assembly hasn’t authorized. The board members who voted for the budget noted the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/columnists/2026/07/31/emanuel-chris-welch-chicago-teachers-union-public-schools-cps-ctu-rich-miller" >speaker of the House</a> and Senate president have publicly indicated a willingness to get more state funding for CPS this year, and including the extra $150 million averted the need to lay off roughly <a class="Link" href="https://news.wttw.com/2026/07/30/cps-board-members-pass-last-minute-amended-budget-assuming-150m-more-state-revenue" target="_blank" >760 teachers, 800 or so support personnel and 41 assistant principals</a>.</p><p>Those who opposed the budget aver it’s not fiscally prudent to bake dollars into CPS spending that haven’t been appropriated by state lawmakers and could hurt the CPS credit rating. While acknowledging key state legislative leaders have voiced support for bumping Illinois investment in CPS, the board members who voted no emphasize those legislative leaders haven’t identified any specific dollar amount of additional funding. They’re also concerned the political pathway to getting more money for CPS is difficult, especially during the veto session, when a supermajority vote is required to pass legislation.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-860000" name="module-860000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnists bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2><br><i>In-depth political coverage, sports analysis, entertainment reviews and cultural commentary.</i><br></div> </div><p>The imbroglio over the CPS budget is heated. But if everyone takes a deep breath, it also affords a rare opportunity to consider fiscal concerns in context of the larger public policy issues being implicated — in this case, education funding.</p><p>In 2017, Illinois replaced its former school funding formula, which was then derided as the least-equitable in the country, with the<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/columnists/2024/08/02/illinois-fully-funding-public-schools-evidence-based-formula-education" > Evidence-Based Funding for Student Success Act</a> or EBF. The EBF ties school funding to covering the cost of those educational practices that research shows actually enhance student achievement, on everything from test scores, to graduation rates and college matriculation rates. Tying taxpayer dollars to paying for what’s been proven to work academically is really good public policy.</p><p>When it passed, the funding formula called for the state to fully fund it within 10 years, which would be this year. But that hasn’t happened. In fact, the aggregate shortfall in K-12 funding has increased each of the last three years and currently sits at $4.2 billion. That means most Illinois school districts — including CPS — still don’t have the resources needed to fund those educational practices the research shows work.</p><p>So why’s that problematic? Well, over the last few decades, the economic importance of educational attainment has grown significantly. All the data shows that individuals with college degrees have lower rates of unemployment and higher incomes than those who don’t complete college. </p><h3>Shortchanging students</h3><p>Consider that in 1979, the median earnings of full-time workers with a bachelor’s degree <a class="Link" href="https://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/speech/bernanke20070206a.htm" target="_blank" >were 38% greater</a> on average than workers with just a high school diploma. By 2024, that wage gap had jumped to 84%. Moreover, communities with a greater number of college-educated folks have lower crime rates, better overall health and higher wages for all workers, not just those with postsecondary degrees. The Federal Reserve of Cleveland even found that states with the best high school and college graduation rates also have the highest per capita personal incomes.</p><p>And this trend isn’t going away. The Georgetown University Center on Education and the Workforce found by 2031, <a class="Link" href="https://cew.georgetown.edu/cew-reports/projections2031/" target="_blank" >72% of jobs</a> will require some postsecondary education credential. Which in turn means the K-12 education students receive has to be of sufficient quality for them to develop the numeracy and literacy skills needed to graduate and gain that post-high school credential. Hence, shortchanging public schools equates to shortchanging the ability of the students who attend them to make it in the modern economy.</p><p>So who are the students being shortchanged? In the case of CPS, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2024/05/14/cps-chicagoans-school-grade-students-not-learning-enough-survey" >71% are low-income</a>, 80% are Black or Brown, and <a class="Link" href="https://www.cps.edu/about/stats-facts/" target="_blank" >27%</a> are English learners. The vast majority of these children have been denied opportunity throughout their young lives. Getting a quality K-12 education, however, will arm them with the academic skills needed to pursue higher education and become qualified for the type of jobs that’ll make them economically self-sufficient.</p><p>Unfortunately, last year CPS <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2025/07/23/chicago-public-schools-budget-deficit" >had $985 million</a> less than what the evidence indicated it needed to provide an adequate education to its students. So those board members who approved the new CPS budget decided to put some pressure on state lawmakers to close $150 million of that gap this year.</p><p>And if the additional state funding doesn’t materialize? CPS could offset the shortage by implementing the roughly $145 million in cuts from furlough days and midyear hiring freezes it previously identified but put off implementing until it sees whether the General Assembly steps up to the plate. That seems, well reasonable, even if not ideal from a pure budgetary policy standpoint.</p><p><i>Ralph Martire is executive director of the Center for Tax and Budget Accountability, a nonpartisan fiscal policy think tank, and the Arthur Rubloff Professor of Public Policy at Roosevelt University.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-130000" name="module-130000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Firms linked to 2 men convicted of corruption have gotten campaign business from JB Pritzker and the CTU
entries.summary: <p>Two political campaign firms with close ties to men with public corruption convictions have gotten business in recent years in Chicago and statewide political races, including the current, hotly contested race for Chicago School Board president and more than $1.5 million from Gov. JB Pritzker in his gubernatorial campaigns, records show.</p><p>In the governor’s campaigns, about $1.2 million went to a firm formed by a former Illinois Department of Children and Family Services deputy director, Bamani Obadele, who pleaded guilty in 2010 to a state contracting scheme under former Gov. Rod Blagojevich. Obadele was sentenced to six months in jail and ordered to repay more than $80,000.</p><p>Pritzker’s gubernatorial campaigns also spent more than $420,000 with the firm tied to Isaac “Ike” Carothers, a former Chicago City Council member who pleaded guilty in 2010 to taking $40,000 in home improvements from a developer who wanted to build homes in an industrial area in Carothers’ 29th Ward on the West Side.</p><p>In the school board race, the Chicago Teachers Union has spent more than $36,000 with the two firms and a company tied to a campaign worker, Karina Escobar-Perez, who pleaded guilty last year to forging signatures on campaign petitions in Indiana for the presidential race. The CTU work was for the campaign of Hilario Dominguez, whom the teachers union endorsed in June for school board president in a five-way race.</p><p>Dominguez’ campaign has reported $99,500 in contributions as of its latest filings, on Aug. 5. All of that was in-kind contributions from the CTU, and about one-third was to firms linked to Obadele, Carothers and Escobar-Perez.</p><p>The CTU’s political organization has used Carothers’ and Obadele’s firms in other school board races, and all three companies have done extensive work in other political races.</p><p>The Dominguez campaign did not respond to questions about the firms.</p><p>The governor’s campaign did not answer questions about Obadele’s and Carothers’ work but said: “The campaign hires consultants who are experienced and well-known organizers in their communities.”</p><p>A CTU spokeswoman said the people and groups they contracted with as “vendors are the same as those hired by Gov. Pritzker, Rep. [Margaret] Croke, and numerous other candidates.” In her statement, she didn't explain those choices, focusing instead on their endorsed candidates: "What voters should know about the candidates we are supporting is that they will be the fiercest advocates for Chicago's children instead of administrators of unnecessary cuts to their education.”</p><p>Pritzker is seeking reelection this year, again running against Republican Darren Bailey, whom he defeated by more than 12 percentage points in 2022. In 2018, Pritzker defeated incumbent Gov. Bruce Rauner by more than 15 percentage points.</p><p>Pritzker, who was among contenders to be Kamala Harris’ 2024 vice presidential running mate, has been attending political events across the country amid speculation he might run for president in 2028.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" records. He admitted in federal court that in 2004 and 2005, when he was at DCFS, he steered contractors working for the state agency to buy promotional items from a company he owned and overcharged them, using proceeds for personal expenses, including an all-expenses-paid vacation for himself and friends to Jamaica. Separately, he admitted having generated business for a company whose board he sat on by telling DCFS contractors to hire the firm.</p><p>Records show Pritzker’s campaign paid Obadele’s firm more than $1 million during the 2022 election, though that spending appears to have escaped notice during the last election. So far, in the governor’s race, the campaign has spent $76,000 with the company, state records show.</p><p>Since 2015, just under half of all the state and local campaign cash that went to Obadele’s firm came from Pritzker’s campaign organization. Pritzker started using Obadele’s firm in 2022.</p><p>The CTU spent more than $16,000 with Obadele’s firm for work on behalf of Dominguez’ campaign. The union also gave his firm $5,250 for work related to Katherine Dunneback’s campaign in school board District 9b. The union endorsed Dunneback and<a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/07/13/ctu-endorses-15-school-board-candidates-throwing-weight-behind-incumbents-mayoral-picks" > a slate of other school board candidates</a> in July.</p><p>In 2018, Illinois Attorney General Kwame Raoul came under scrutiny for spending $13,000 with Obadele for campaign work.</p><p>Obadele said his work on campaigns includes a variety of get-out-the-vote efforts across the South Side and elsewhere in Cook County. “I have done this the past 15 years with fidelity,” he wrote in response to questions.</p><p>In a written statement in response to questions, Obadele defended the work he’s done: “I’m neither ashamed nor proud of my past conviction. I paid my debt to society and have remained committed to pushing forward in a positive and impactful way. Since then, I have built and operated a successful professional business … This work has provided hundreds of individuals, including those who face barriers to employment. I stand for and believe in second chances and the importance of allowing people who have also paid their debt to society to receive the same opportunities I too was given."</p><p>Obadele is also the “community and civic engagement director” for Acclivus Inc., a community health organization focused on violence prevention that has had dozens of state contracts in recent years worth more than $100 million, including $16 million in contracts for this fiscal year with the Illinois Department of Human Services and the Illinois Department of Commerce and Economic Opportunity.</p><p>Obadele said he doesn’t run Acclivus, and he's proud to work there because of the anti-violence work it does in Chicago. </p><p>“My role there is to oversee community engagement and workforce development,” he wrote.</p><p>The governor’s office wouldn't comment.</p><p>Sheila Regan, the chief operating officer for Acclivus, said, “It’s unclear what connection could be made between Obadele’s campaign work and Acclivus grants because there is no relationship between them.”</p><p>“All state grants to Acclivus have been awarded in alignment with state law, primarily via competitive grant processes,” she said.</p><p>Obadele’s campaign business has also worked for Mayor Brandon Johnson, Ald. Pat Dowell, state Rep. Kam Buckner, Croke and a Pritzker-backed group that campaigned unsuccessfully for a graduated income tax in 2020.</p><p>Another firm, Senior Wizdom Consulting (which is listed under various spellings in election records), is closely tied to Carothers and was paid more than $366,000 by Pritzker’s gubernatorial campaign in 2022 for “strategic field consulting” and has already made $55,000 for work It also paid Carothers’ firm $3,920 this summer to support Michilla Blaise, the CTU-endorsed candidate in the District 5b Chicago School Board race.</p><p>While dozens of Chicago City Council members have gone to prison, Carothers has the distinction of following in the footsteps of his father, former Ald. William Carothers, who also went to prison in a political corruption scandal.</p><p>Campaign records indicate Carothers has had dozens of other clients over that time as well, including former Cook She pleaded guilty to a felony for the forgeries and was sentenced to a year in prison and a year of probation. Escobar-Perez served one day in custody, and the prison sentence was suspended. Indiana court records show she owes more than $1,100 in fees and fines.</p><p>Escobar-Perez and two companies linked to her have taken in more than $400,000 for campaign-related work since 2020, most of which was from before she was charged. Since Escobar-Perez’ plea deal, the CTU has been one of Moving Forward Strategies’ largest clients.</p><p>Escobar-Perez did not return a written request for comment but told a police investigator she felt pressured to turn in the Indiana campaign petitions within a five-day deadline, according to a police report.</p>

entries.title: One down, one to go: Exterior construction wraps up at the first of two towers at 400 N. Lake Shore
entries.summary: <p>After more than two years of construction, Chicagoans can now see what the residential tower built on the spot of the proposed Chicago Spire will look like — from the outside, at least — once completed.</p><p>Exterior construction wrapped up late last month on the 72-story skyscraper at 400 N. Lake Shore Drive, with the installation of the building's last piece of facade glass.</p><p>That means what we now see of the 857-foot tall glass building is what we'll get. Crews are building out the interior and surrounding grounds.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-7f0000" name="image-7f0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/fd78427/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6123x3436+0+323/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fd1%2Fae%2F8329349a4d90a095f1cd3d4b89c0%2F400lsd-260810-08.JPG 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/d04c776/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6123x3436+0+323/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fd1%2Fae%2F8329349a4d90a095f1cd3d4b89c0%2F400lsd-260810-08.JPG 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/08bcdbc/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6123x3436+0+323/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fd1%2Fae%2F8329349a4d90a095f1cd3d4b89c0%2F400lsd-260810-08.JPG" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="A close-up of the cascading, waterfall-like windows of one of the towers at 400 N. Lake Shore Drive.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>"Seeing that profile in the skyline is pretty remarkable," said Ann Thompson, executive vice president of architecture and design at Related Midwest, the company developing the site. "You're seeing a fully completed exterior."</p><p>Still, it's worth making note of this milestone in the project's construction. Until the current project kicked off in 2024, the site was best known for the circular 75-foot deep crater left there when a previous plan to build a spiraling 2,000-foot tall building designed by architect and engineer Santiago Calatrava went belly up in 2008.</p><p>The plan calls for a 60-story near-twin tower to be built 75 feet to the south. But construction on the second building won't begin until at least a year after the current tower is fully leased — and if real estate market forces are charitable.</p><p>"[That] gives us a lot of information to work on for the second tower, in terms of the demographics and how is the site functioning," Thompson said. "It allows us to use that information to inform the second building ... particularly the interiors of the second tower."</p><p>The building that's there now is a slender glass building with a facade that steps back — almost cascades — as it rises.</p><p>The skyscrapers and its planned companion sit on the west side of DuSable Lake Shore Drive near the mouth of the Ogden Slip, a former industrial harbor that runs parallel to the last lengths of the Chicago River.</p><p>Current work on the 400 N. Lake Shore site includes installing trees, bushes and plantings on the north side of the property.</p><p>A sculpture by a major artist — whom Thompson wouldn't name — is planned.</p><p>And the finished Founders Way, an important extension of the Riverwalk that leads past 400 N. Lake Shore, runs below DuSable Lake Shore Drive and will ultimately connect to the yet-to-be constructed $15 million <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/architecture-design/2025/04/23/dusable-park-development-chicago-takes-a-step-forward" target="_blank" >DuSable Park</a>, Thompson said.</p><p>Related Midwest is covering $10 million of the park's $15 million cost.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" Lake Shore Drive. Exterior work on the north tower is complete.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Provided by Related Midwest</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>What do I think of the building?</p><p>I'm holding off until it's completed sometime in 2027. But I will say, the building has an overall power and elegance that could be diminished if the second tower isn't built.</p><p>And I have to say this, though: SOM claims the waterfall-like windows are a modern interpretation of the classic Chicago bay window. But as a person who grew up in a house with a two-story bay window, I struggle to see the visual connection.</p><p>That's not a knock against 400 N. Lake Shore's windows. They are among the building's better features.</p><p>And it's no Chicago Spire — nor does it have to be, said Chicago Architecture Center CEO Eleanor Gorski, an architect and former high-ranking city planning official.</p><p>"You see [buildings like this] being pursued all in the Middle East and Far East," she said. "But I almost feel like Chicago has outgrown having to do that. I think that we take advantage of whatever scale we have and look for the best architectural outcomes."</p><p>Gorski added, "Frankly from an urban design standpoint, I think it maybe it would have been a little gruesome to have this gigantic tower there."</p>

entries.title: National pediatrics group says all kids 6 months and older should receive flu shot
entries.summary: <p>The American Academy of Pediatrics is urging children ages 6 months and older receive this year's flu shot. The Illinois-based organization is making the recommendation before any federal agencies release their own guidelines for the upcoming flu season.</p><p>Last year, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention removed its long-time universal recommendation for the annual flu shot from its childhood vaccine schedule. Instead, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2026/01/05/us-drops-the-number-of-vaccines-it-recommends-for-every-child" target="_blank" >the CDC only said</a> certain "high-risk" groups need to get the shot or when doctors recommend it in what’s called “shared decision-making.”</p><p>In the organization's statement, the pediatric organization emphasized the safety and benefits of the shot, especially after nearly 200 children died from the flu during the 2025-2026 flu season. Yet less than 50% of children ages 6 months to 17 years were vaccinated, according to the the group.</p><p>“The good news is flu vaccines have been thoroughly studied,” said Dr. Kristina Bryant, a member of the American Academy of Pediatrics' Committee on Infectious Diseases.</p><p>“We know they are safe in children and they can prevent not just hospitalizations and death but every year they prevent a substantial number of illnesses that result in trips to the doctor’s office," Bryant said in a statement. "We want to keep kids healthy and going to school and parents healthy and going to work. Flu vaccines can help us accomplish that.”</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://publications.aap.org/pediatrics/article-abstract/158/2/e2026076453/208191/Influenza-Vaccine-Effectiveness-Against-Pediatric?redirectedFrom=fulltext" target="_blank" >A recent CDC study</a> found the flu shot reduces the risk of kids and teens dying from the virus by 80%. During the 2024-2025 flu season, <a class="Link" href="https://www.cdc.gov/flu-burden/php/data-vis-vac/index.html" target="_blank" >the CDC estimates</a> the vaccine prevented nearly 15,000 hospitalizations and 245 deaths in children and teens.</p><p>The American Academy of Pediatrics noted the CDC has yet to release new flu vaccine recommendations.</p><p>The pediatrics group recommends that children receive the vaccine as soon as it becomes available — ideally by the end of October, ahead of flu season. Pregnant and breastfeeding people are also encouraged to get the shot to protect themselves and their infants.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2025/09/10/covid-19-vaccines-arrive-at-chicago-pharmacies-as-pediatricians-wait-for-doses-and-guidance" target="_blank" >Pediatricians have previously told the Sun-Times</a> it's best for everyone to get their flu shot just before winter because the vaccine works best in the eight to 12 weeks after getting it.</p>

entries.title: Man who died nearly a month after being shot in West Englewood identified
entries.summary: <p>A man who died nearly a month after he was shot in West Englewood has been identified. </p><p>Edward L. Ford, 52, was in an argument in the 6000 block of South Damen Avenue around 5:15 p.m. June 27 when he was shot in the body multiple times, Chicago police and the Cook County medical examiner's office said. </p><p>Ford was taken to the University of Chicago Medical Center in critical condition and died July 23 due to complications from multiple gunshot wounds, officials said. </p><p>A 26-year-old man was taken into custody and two firearms were recovered at the scene. </p>

entries.title: Claire's revamps piercing experience for Gen Alpha, but brand nostalgia spans generations
entries.summary: <p>Teen accessories and jewelry retailer Claire’s said its stores will undergo a “glow-up,” one year after it filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy. </p><p>The company, which moved from Hoffman Estates to Rosemont earlier this summer, plans to invest in its piercing services and in-store experience, starting this month. The transformation will happen across Claire’s 900 locations in the U.S. and Canada, according to a news release. The Chicago area has 19 locations, including one at Water Tower Place. </p><p>“We really do see [piercing] as a responsibility, not just a service," Claire's Vice President of Retail Operations Carey Brezler said. “It is a milestone moment, and it's a rite of passage for so many. ... We always say that it's a transformation. Since it's founding more than 50 years ago, over 131 million people have pierced their ears at Claire's, the company said.</p><p>Growing up in South Bend, Indiana, my mother brought me to the local Claire's when I was 4 years old. I left that day with a pink Dora the Explorer wallet, stickers and pierced ears.</p><p>It became a stop during mall days a decade later with friends. At 19, I went back with my best friend for another ear piercing. </p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a grandmother.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Provided by Mariah Rush</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>But the retailer didn't start out with piercing services. In 1973, Chicago native Rowland Schaefer, owner of wig business Fashion Tress Wigs, acquired Claire's Boutiques as part of a move to shift into the accessories business, the <a class="Link" href="https://www.wsj.com/articles/SB10001424127887324412604578513682190931990" target="_blank" >Wall Street Journal</a> reported. He soon began tailoring the merchandise to preteens and teens, and the business was renamed to Claire’s Accessories.</p><p>A Claire’s opened in the South Bend area the same year it was founded. My mother was 16 at the time. She wanted to get her nose pierced, against her parents' wishes. While Claire’s didn’t offer piercings until 1978, they had sold a self-piercing kit, which my mother said she purchased. Soon after, she was sporting a nose stud and avoiding her parents.</p><p>My mother, now 68, remembers frequenting Claire’s throughout high school, and a decade later for an ear piercing.</p><p>“It was the only place in town with affordable, cool jewelry and accessories,” she said.</p><p>My grandmother, 96, is equally rebellious, and found her way to Claire's. </p><p>When she was 93, she decided she wanted to get her ears pierced again so she could wear earrings. My grandmother directed her at-home helper to make a stop at the mall and requested to be taken to Claire’s — getting her piercing at the same store I had decades earlier. She told the family after it was done.</p><p>With this new transformation, Claire’s is hoping to create a similar experience for a new generation. Their plan includes store redesigns, as well as clinical training for piercing staff and FDA-registered medical devices. Shoppers will be able to visit an interactive "inspiration bar” to build an earrings stack, take Instagram selfies and squeeze stress toys during piercings to help ease anxiety or fear, according to have grown in popularity with trendy accessories and colorful store interiors.</p><p>The company is also trying to move past its operational struggles that led to its <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/money/2025/08/07/claires-piercing-teens-ears-chapter-11-bankruptcy" >second bankruptcy</a>. Its court filing said it had assets and liabilities ranging between $1 billion and $10 billion. </p><p>“Increased competition, consumer spending trends and the ongoing shift away from brick-and-mortar retail, in combination with our current debt obligations and macroeconomic factors, necessitate this course of action for Claire’s and its stakeholders," Clarie's CEO Chris Cramer said at the time.</p><p>Maryland-based private equity firm Ames Watson acquired the company in September 2025 for $140 million, with plans to modernize the retail chain, according to a news release from the firm. </p><p>“One of the things that we have to remember too is that Claire's itself was a troubled company, but it wasn't a troubled brand” Brezler said. “There is so much brand resonance. You talk to anybody, and you say, 'I work for Claire's.' It's unreal how many stories there are.”</p><p>She said Chicago-area locations will be updated by the end of August. Its flagship location at Woodfield Mall will be updated early September.</p><p>And its deep purple hue, familiar to older generations, has been replaced with what's described as a “Gen Alpha-approved shade of purple,” called lilith. And there’s a new tagline — “I got pierced at Claire’s.”</p><p>"When we talk about the Claire's girl, it's myself, it's you, it's your grandmother, sister, your aunt, your mother ... because it's entries.title: Bears WR Luther Burden's groin injury expected to keep him out this preseason: report
entries.summary: <p>Luther Burden’s groin injury is expected to keep him out for the rest of the preseason, ESPN’s Adam Schefter reported Monday.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> receiver limped off the field during practice Saturday after leaping for a pass in the end zone during a one-on-one drill against cornerback Tyrique Stevenson. He <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/08/09/bears-training-camp-luther-burden-groin-injury-nfl-sits-out-wide-receiver-zavion-thomas" target="_blank" >did not practice Sunday.</a> The Bears start their season Sept. 13 at the Panthers, and hope to have Burden with them.</p><p>Until then, the Bears will give extra snaps to Jahdae Walker and rookie Zavion Thomas, both who are locks to make the team. Lesser-known receivers having strong camps include Kaden Davis and J.P. Richardson. They figure to play a lot in the Bears' first preseason game Saturday against the Browns at Soldier Field. Coach Ben Johnson doesn't seem likely to play his starters much, if at all.</p><p>Burden's absence, though, is a blow for an offense trying to make a leap in Year 2 under Johnson. Burden has been a trendy pick this offseason, both inside and outside Halas Hall, to emerge as a star. Johnson said in June that “I’m buying Luther Burden stock right now,” while general manager Ryan Poles said in July that “if there’s a guy I’m really excited about, it’s Luther Burden.”</p><p>Burden had 47 catches on 60 targets for 652 yards and two touchdowns last year. In the last three weeks of the regular season alone, he caught 17 passes for 257 yards.</p>

the eulogy and ended her mother's funeral service at the South Chicago Chapel, 2939 E. 95th St., Thursday when Chicago police blocked her and her family's vehicles. Not long after, <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydllhriy-l-q/" target="_blank" >officers found dozens of decomposing bodies inside the funeral home</a>. Some were crammed into closets and in a nearby garage, police said. "I trusted them with my mom's remains," Johnson told the Sun-Times. The Cook County medical examiner's office said it was assessing the remains of 56 people.</p><p><b>History of mishandling</b>: The discovery of the bodies in the South Deering funeral home <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydllhriy-l-a/" target="_blank" >was not the first time Clark and Johanna Morgan, the business operators, were found to have mishandled remains</a>. Last year, state officials shut down the Morgans' Chicago Heights crematory amid allegations they had mishandled around 100 bodies there. Nearly two dozen lawsuits were filed against the Morgans, but they continued to operate South Chicago Chapel.</p><p><b>Man's body released</b>: Keith Allen Young’s funeral was supposed to be Friday. Instead, his family spent part of the day at the medical examiner's office trying to locate his body because <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydllhriy-l-f/" target="_blank" >the funeral home never delivered it to the church</a>. As officials work to identify the bodies removed from South Chicago Chapel, Young's sister said the family learned on Saturday that his body could finally be released.</p><p><b>Cemetery investigated​​​​​​</b>: In an unrelated investigation, the Illinois comptroller's office announced it's <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydllhriy-l-z/" target="_blank" >looking into Bohemian National Cemetery</a> after a tip last month led officials to find equipment failures and remains href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydllhriy-l-dl/" target="_blank" >Bud Billiken Parade marks 97 years of tradition</a></h3><p></p><h5>Reporting by <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydllhriy-l-dr/" target="_blank" >Cindy Hernandez</a></h5><p>Hundreds gathered along Martin Luther King Drive Saturday morning to watch the Bud Billiken Parade step off in Bronzeville and march into Washington Park.</p><p>In its 97th year, the Bud Billiken is one of the largest and longest-running parades in the country. Founded in 1929 by Robert Sengstacke Abbott, publisher and founder of the Chicago Defender, the parade was created to celebrate Black children and their achievements.</p><p>The parade features marching bands, floats, dance teams, community organizations and youth groups. The route, roughly two miles long, started at Pershing Road and headed south down King Drive toward Washington Park, ending at Garfield Boulevard.</p><p>In addition to the local and state politicians who marched in the parade, this year's Grand Marshal was actress LisaRaye McCoy.</p><p>Paradegoers told the Sun-Times the Bud Billiken is both a back-to-school tradition and a celebration of South Side pride.</p><p>Jasmine and Devon Hughes, both 33, said they attended the parade as children and always had a good time. Saturday marked the first time they brought their two young children, continuing the tradition with the next generation.</p><p>"It’s a blessing that it’s gone on for so long, and hopefully it can go another 97 years without the tradition being broken," Devon Hughes said.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydllhriy-l-dy/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p></p><h4>YOUR DAILY QUESTION ☕️</h4><p><b>What's your favorite monument in Chicago? entries.title: Every known federal prosecution in Chicago tied to Trump’s immigration blitz
entries.summary: <p>Federal prosecutors in Chicago have accused 33 known defendants of nonimmigration crimes tied to Operation Midway Blitz. Many were accused of assaulting or resisting federal agents or officers.</p><p>Two defendants have pleaded guilty. Twenty-five have been cleared. Grand jurors refused to indict at least three of the 25, and another member of that group was found not guilty at trial.</p><p>One of the 25 saw their charges dropped through a deferred-prosecution agreement. Under the terms of such a deal, prosecutors agree to drop charges if a defendant abides by certain terms over a set period of time. Five Midway Blitz defendants struck such a deal, and four are still pending.</p><p>The Chicago Sun-Times is tracking all of the known criminal cases tied to Operation Midway Blitz:</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-6e0000" name="html-embed-module-6e0000"></a><div class="flourish-embed flourish-table" data-src="visualisation/27349648"><script src="https://public.flourish.studio/resources/embed.js"></script><noscript><img src="https://public.flourish.studio/visualisation/27349648/thumbnail" width="100%" alt="table visualization" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><div class="PageListO" data-module data-show-loadmore="true" ><a class="AnchorLink" id="list-bb0000" name="list-bb0000"></a> <div class="PageList-header" > <div class="PageList-header-title-wrap" > <div class="PageList-header-title"> Latest from Jon Seidel </div> </div> </div> <div class="PageListO-items"> <div class="PageListO-items-row"> <div class="PageListO-items-column" data-with-borders> <div class="PageListO-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/07/29/loretto-hospital-fraud-anosh-ahmed-broadview-six" >Indicted ex-Loretto exec’s return to U.S. could add to feds’ 'Broadview 6' headaches</a> </div> <div class="PageListO-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/madigan-trial-news/2026/07/29/michael-madigan-supreme-court-appeal" >Former Illinois House Speaker Michael Madigan asks U.S. Supreme Court to hear his corruption case</a> </div> <div class="PageListO-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/07/28/judge-threat-sara-ellis-james-lebuhn" >Libertyville man gets 6 months in prison for threatening federal judges with photos of bullets</a> </div> </div> </div> </div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Hallan 57 cuerpos en descomposición en funeraria del extremo sur de Chicago
entries.summary: <p>Varios cadáveres fueron cargados en vehículos la mañana del viernes, aparentemente trasladados a la Oficina del Médico Forense del Condado de Cook, después de que docenas de cuerpos en descomposición fueron hallados en una funeraria del extremo sur de la ciudad.</p><p>Los reporteros del Chicago Sun-Times vieron cómo los restos de al menos tres cadáveres eran colocados en una SUV sin distintivos frente a la South Chicago Chapel, en 2939 E. 95th St., alrededor de las 9 a.m. Se cargaron más restos en otro vehículo.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div normativa estatal, según un reporte de policía obtenido por el Sun-Times.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-1e0000" los familiares dijeron que la funeraria debía entregar el cuerpo de su ser querido a la iglesia para un velorio el jueves, pero el cuerpo nunca llegó.</p><p>Los oficiales fueron recibidos por el director funerario, Clark Morgan, quien los acompañó en una inspección del edificio, según el reporte de policía. Durante la inspección encontraron 57 cuerpos en distintas áreas de la funeraria. Los cuerpos no estaban refrigerados y presentaban distintos grados de descomposición.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure Deering.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Tyler Pasciak LaRiviere/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>En determinado momento los oficiales salieron del edificio y, cuando intentaron volver a entrar, Morgan les dijo que por consejo de su abogado, no les permitiría reingresar sin una orden. Tras decirles a los oficiales que no necesitaban una orden para inspeccionar el edificio durante el horario de atención, cerró la puerta con un candado y se marchó, según el reporte. Los oficiales llamaron entonces al Departamento de Bomberos de Chicago para que ayudara a forzar la entrada al edificio.</p><p>La licencia del negocio fue revocada el miércoles, según el reporte de policía. No estaba claro al principio por qué la policía no visitó la funeraria hasta el día siguiente.</p><p>En un comunicado el viernes, la contralora de Illinois, Susana Mendoza, dijo que, aunque la South Chicago Chapel no está bajo la jurisdicción de su oficina, sí conoce a los operadores de la funeraria, Johanna y Clark Morgan, por sus "prácticas pasadas atroces mientras operaban Heights Crematory", lo cual es similar a la situación de 2025.</p><p>"Horrorizada. Otra vez. El descubrimiento de restos en descomposición, a la espera de ser enterrados esta semana en una funeraria del lado sur, es desgarrador y una abominación. Son personas —la madre, el padre, la hermana, el hermano, el hijo o el amigo de alguien— y merecen algo mejor", destacó Mendoza en el comunicado.</p><p>La oficina de la contralora de Illinois <a class="Link" href="https://illinoiscomptroller.gov/newsroom/press-releases/comptroller-mendoza-permanently-closes-heights-crematory-through-consent-order" target="_blank" >cerró definitivamente</a> Heights Crematory en Chicago Heights el año pasado después de que los investigadores encontraron varios cuerpos mal almacenados y cientos de restos cremados que "nunca habían sido devueltos a sus familias", dijo Mendoza en el comunicado. Los Morgan también administraban ese negocio.</p><p>"Muchos de los cuerpos estaban apilados unos sobre otros, no estaban refrigerados y estaban parcialmente expuestos. Las cremaciones se retrasaron y el registro de datos era pésimo”, dijo Mendoza en el comunicado. "Que estos mismos operadores estén haciendo lo mismo otra vez en South Chicago Chapel Funeral Home es indignante".</p><p>El alcalde Brandon Johnson, en un comunicado emitido el viernes por la mañana, dijo que los informes son "profundamente perturbadores".</p><p>"Las familias confiaron en esta funeraria para el cuidado de sus seres queridos en uno de los momentos más difíciles de sus vidas. Esa confianza parece haber sido profundamente traicionada", destacó el alcalde en el comunicado.</p><p>"Cada persona merece ser tratada con dignidad en la vida y en la muerte, y cada familia merece compasión, transparencia y respeto mientras lamenta su pérdida", enfatizó.</p><p>"A medida que continúa esta investigación, nuestros corazones están con cada familia que busca respuestas", dijo el alcalde en el comunicado. "Esperamos que reciban la claridad que merecen y la tranquilidad de saber que sus seres queridos serán enterrados con la dignidad, el cuidado y el respeto que toda persona merece".</p><p>El área alrededor de la funeraria fue acordonada por la policía el jueves por la noche mientras los vecinos rondaban el lugar. Al menos una persona fue a la escena para preguntarles a los oficiales si habían encontrado los restos de su madre. El funeral fue el 18 de julio y la mujer dijo que la funeraria había evitado responder sus llamadas el jueves.</p><p>Le habían dicho que tendría acceso a los restos cremados de su madre menos de dos semanas después del funeral. Ya casi se cumplían tres semanas.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-e7d98b" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>La Policía de Chicago investiga la South Chicago Chapel tras hallarse el jueves decenas de cuerpos en descomposición en toda la funeraria.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Tyler Pasciak LaRiviere/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>La persona dijo que había notado un olor cuando fue anteriormente, pero lo atribuyó al olor del líquido de embalsamamiento.</p><p>"Estaba en paz, había pasado un mes", dijo.</p><p>"Ahora", dijo, con la voz apagada, "Solo espero que no esté ahí, pero algo me dice que sí".</p><p>El olor fétido que se percibía la noche del jueves empezó durante el invierno, dijeron varios vecinos al Sun-Times.</p><p>Un par de vecinos dijo que les sorprendían las horas tardías a las que la gente trabajaba en la funeraria. Un vecino que trabajaba en turno nocturno dijo que con frecuencia veía vehículos en el estacionamiento pasada la medianoche y una luz encendida en el piso de arriba de la funeraria.</p><p>Los vecinos contaron que colocaron trampas para atrapar las miles de moscas que emanaban del edificio. Ellos, junto con otros vecinos, denunciaron la situación ante las autoridades hace seis meses.</p><p>"Estamos agradecidos", dijo un vecino sobre la investigación. "Me parecía raro… [Pero] teníamos una idea de lo que estaba pasando".</p><p>En un comunicado, la Oficina del Médico Forense del Condado de Cook dijo que su personal está "evaluando las condiciones de los restos, buscando documentación relacionada con la identificación de los fallecidos así como los certificados de defunción. Este proceso podría tardar varios días en asegurar la disposición adecuada. La oficina trabajará con las autoridades para identificar a estos fallecidos lo más rápido posible y notificar a sus familias".</p><p>Otra vecina dijo que cuando la gente entraba o salía del edificio para un funeral, "se olía la podredumbre".</p><p>"Al principio pensamos que venía de una fábrica cercana, pero olía a descomposición", agregó otra vecina. "Olor a un animal muerto… No fue una o dos veces, fue todos los fines de semana. Era una lucha salir a la calle y subirse al auto".</p><p>"Sólo esperamos que las familias encuentren a sus seres queridos", agregó.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div entries.title: Tim Anderson announces retirement from baseball with White Sox, who will honor him Sept. 17
entries.summary: <p>Tim Anderson announced his retirement from baseball Monday, and the White Sox will honor him before the game Sept. 17, when the team will wear its original "Southside" City Connect uniforms. </p><p>Anderson, 33, made his announcement on a Zoom call, during which he said baseball brought him a lot of good moments but also a lot of pain. He was visibly sweating on the screen and needed to wipe his face. </p><p>"Definitely a lot of dark moments," Anderson said. "Got to a point where I couldn’t enjoy it. You see I'm sweating. I still love the game; it just brought too much pain for me. So going back to play is not for me right now in life."</p><p>The good moments include two All-Star Game appearances (2021, 2022), one Silver Slugger Award (2020) and one American League batting title. They also include one of the most memorable home runs in Sox history, Anderson's walk-off homer against the Yankees in the 2021 "Field of Dreams" game.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Tim Anderson was special. 😮‍💨<br><br>(Via: <a href="https://x.com/MLBONFOX?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">@MLBONFOX</a>) <a href="https://t.co/RuEFKgWL4L">pic.twitter.com/RuEFKgWL4L</a></p>— Foul Territory (@FoulTerritoryTV) <a href="https://x.com/FoulTerritoryTV/status/2086854073186205753?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">August 10, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>The bad moments came later. His play began to suffer in 2023, when he hit one home run and batted .245. The Sox granted him free agency after the season. He played 65 games for the Marlins in 2024 and 31 for the Angels in 2025. </p><p>Also in 2023, he got knocked down in a fight at second base with the Guardians' Jose Ramirez, and he shared that he had had a child out of wedlock and was working through it with his wife, Bria.</p><p>Anderson said the Sox invited him to throw out a ceremonial first pitch at a game this season. That's when he brought up his plan to retire with the Sox. He said he's much happier in his post-baseball life.</p><p>"I get to wake up every day being happy," said Anderson, who has a food truck and is working on a clothing line. "Don’t gotta wake up hitting no curveball."</p><div class="PageListL" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" data-show-loadmore="true" ><a class="AnchorLink" id="list-4a0005" name="list-4a0005"></a><div class="PageList-header" > <div class="PageList-header-title-wrap" > <div class="PageList-header-title"> <a class="" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="{borderColor=#dfdfdf, pageNumber=1, inverseColors=false, count=10144, items=[{type=Image, wordCount=645, title=Hagen Smith earns first major-league victory in first appearance for White Sox, description=[{items=[Smith struck out the side in the second inning before walking the bases loaded in the third and escaping. entries.title: 15-year-old boy fatally shot in West Garfield Park identified
entries.summary: <p>A 15-year-old boy who was fatally shot in West Garfield Park last month has been identified. </p><p>Officers responded to calls of a person shot around 1 a.m. July 22 in the 4600 block of West Jackson Boulevard and found Lasiah Alexander Palmer with a gunshot wound to his head, Chicago police and the Cook County medical examiner's office said. </p><p>He was taken to Stroger Hospital where he was pronounced dead, police said. </p><p>Area 4 detectives were investigating. </p>

entries.title: Shops at North Bridge will get $40 million makeover
entries.summary: <p>The Shops at North Bridge will receive a<b> </b>$40 million facelift and a new strategy to entice experiential, or interactive, retailers to open at the sprawling six-block shopping mall.</p><p>Construction on the interior will start this month, followed by exterior work. The renovations are expected to position the mall, at 520 N. Michigan Ave., as a “premier, experience-driven destination,” the mall announced last week.</p><p>“At The Shops at North Bridge, we’re investing in the future of experiential urban retail and the continued evolution of Michigan Avenue as a global destination,” Deb Mattes, senior general manager at Centennial, the mall’s management company, said in a news release. “This redevelopment is designed to create a stronger sense of arrival, encourage visitors to spend more time within the property and deliver an experience that reflects the energy and international appeal of Chicago.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-410000" name="image-410000"></a> <picture entries.title: City treasurer proposes abolishing $57M Catalyst Fund to avert midyear layoffs
entries.summary: <p>City Treasurer Melissa Conyears-Ervin wants to disband a fund created a decade ago to jump-start development in South and West Side neighborhoods, and use the remaining $57 million to prevent the city’s midyear budget shortfall from triggering police and fire department layoffs.</p><p>Even before confronting the $1 billion hole in next year’s budget, Chicago faces a $90 million midyear shortfall after alternative revenue approved over Mayor Brandon Johnson’s objections fell short.</p><p>Before resigning their jobs in rapid-fire succession, Budget Director <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/08/03/annette-guzman-brandon-johnson-budget-director" >Annette Guzman</a> and Chief Financial Officer <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/07/28/mayor-brandon-johnson-acting-cfo-steve-mahr-resigns" >Steven Mahr</a> warned of employee layoffs and pulled back on their commitment to make the second half of a $260 million advance pension payment at the center of the budget battle.</p><p>Now, Conyears-Ervin has a plan to eliminate more than half of this the midyear shortfall without laying off police officers and firefighters: Abolish the $57 million “Catalyst Fund” created by onetime Mayor Rahm Emanuel.</p><p>“The city is at a moment where we’re facing an over $90 million deficit. Responsible leadership … means being able to shift. It means recognizing when we need to address what is happening right now,” Conyears-Ervin told the Chicago Sun-Times. “And in this moment, we need to save city services of our police officers, of our firefighters. Residents do not want to hear that police officers and firefighters are going to be laid off.”</p><p>Then-Mayor Rahm Emanuel's 2017 budget included a $100 million "Catalyst Fund" to bridge the funding gap between Chicago's thriving Downtown and other neighborhoods. Then-City Treasurer Kurt Summers assured a skeptical City Council that the $100 million in seed money would be matched by “three times” that much in outside capital. </p><p>He said a seven-member board that included the treasurer would select private managers who would be required to invest the money in low-income neighborhoods and census tracts covered by the Community Reinvestment Act. </p><p>One year later, the Catalyst Fund still had not launched, and board members had not been appointed. Summers proposed that $57 million in excess “portfolio earnings" generated by his office be used to stop violence on Chicago streets — via investing in long-neglected inner-city neighborhoods.</p><p>Still, the Catalyst Fund went nowhere until the pandemic, when then-Mayor Lori Lightfoot forged a partnership with Conyears-Ervin and used the money to provide loans to small businesses fighting for survival.</p><p>Although the Catalyst Fund never lived up to its promise of attracting private investment, Conyears-Ervin said, “We did revive it.”</p><p>“We were able to help 762 small businesses … keep their doors open, keep employees in our community working during the pandemic. That was definitely an impact we were able to make, and it was a social impact that was necessary at that time. The loans have now been repaid in full,” she said. “Right now, I have identified that the greater need is to stave off layoffs for police officers and firefighters and other essential workers." </p><p>The Catalyst Fund was created by City Council ordinance, and only the City Council can disband the fund. Conyears-Ervin would only say that there “will be an ordinance drafted internally” and that she is working to determine who would introduce it.</p><p>“City Council members, I’m sure, would appreciate receiving $57 million toward the over $90 million deficit,” said the treasurer, whose husband is Budget Committee Chair Jason Ervin (28th), Johnson’s most powerful ally.</p><p>Summers could not be reached for comment. Conyears-Ervin's plan to abolish the fund was first reported by Illinois Playbook. Johnson's office had no immediate comment on the treasurer's proposal.</p><p>If he seeks reelection, Johnson could end up avoiding any kind of retreat from his signature promise to pump sorely needed capital into the South and West Side communities he has championed.</p><p>But Conyears-Ervin said, "South and West Side neighborhoods also do not want you to lay off police officers in our communities [where] we know and recognize the need for — as well as firefighters and other essential workers."</p>
